God's care for those who care for the needy (verses 1–4)

God's people are not exempt from poverty, illness or outward suffering. But the Lord considers their condition and gives them what they need in due time.

Following their Master's example, believers learn to show concern for poor and suffering brothers and sisters. This kind of godliness often receives earthly blessings.

Yet nothing troubles a repentant believer more than the fear of God's displeasure or the discovery of sin still living in the heart.

Sin is the sickness of the soul. Pardoning mercy heals its guilt, and renewing grace heals its corruption.

We should therefore seek spiritual healing with greater earnestness than we seek bodily health.

David suffers betrayal and praises God (verses 5–13)

We rightly lament the scarcity of sincere friendship among human beings, but the past was no better.

Someone whom David deeply trusted joined his enemies.

We should not be surprised when people we considered friends treat us badly.

Yet we ourselves have broken promises made to God. We receive food from his hand every day and still raise our heel against him.

We must not delight in the downfall of our enemies. We can, however, rejoice when their harmful plans are defeated.

A mercy becomes doubly precious when we recognize God's favor behind it, whether the blessing concerns one person or the public good.

Without his constant sustaining grace, we could not remain standing.

While still on earth, let us join wholeheartedly in the praise that God's redeemed people offer to their God and Savior both here and in heaven.

[Ps.41.1-Ps.41.4]
Chapter 41
Chapter Outline
God's care for his people. | (1-4) |
The treachery of David's enemies. | (5-13) |
Verses 1-4
The people of God are not free from poverty, sickness, or outward affliction, but the Lord will consider their case, and send due supplies. From his Lord's example the believer learns to consider his poor and afflicted brethren. This branch of godliness is usually recompensed with temporal blessings. But nothing is so distressing to the contrite believer, as a fear or sense of the Divine displeasure, or of sin in his heart. Sin is the sickness of the soul; pardoning mercy heals it, renewing grace heals it, and for this spiritual healing we should be more earnest than for bodily health.
[Ps.41.5-Ps.41.13]
Verses 5-13
We complain, and justly, of the want of sincerity, and that there is scarcely any true friendship to be found among men; but the former days were no better. One particularly, in whom David had reposed great confidence, took part with his enemies. And let us not think it strange, if we receive evil from those we suppose to be friends. Have not we ourselves thus broken our words toward God? We eat of his bread daily, yet lift up the heel against him. But though we may not take pleasure in the fall of our enemies, we may take pleasure in the making vain their designs. When we can discern the Lord's favour in any mercy, personal or public, that doubles it. If the grace of God did not take constant care of us, we should not be upheld. But let us, while on earth, give heartfelt assent to those praises which the redeemed on earth and in heaven render to their God and Saviour.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The conflict in the soul of a believer.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–5Second section6–11
Longing for the living God (verses 1–5)

The psalmist regarded the Lord as his highest good, and directed his heart toward him.

By fixing his anchor there from the beginning, he was able to endure the storm.

A gracious soul cannot be content merely to attend worship if it does not encounter God himself.

Living souls cannot truly rest anywhere short of the living God.

The upright person longs to appear before him; the hypocrite dreads that meeting.

Few things trouble a believer more than attempts to shake confidence in the Lord.

David was not merely missing the pleasures of royal life. He grieved over the free access to God's house he formerly enjoyed and the happiness of worshiping there.

People who search their own hearts often discover thoughts that need correction.

Here is the remedy for sorrow: when the soul relies on itself, it sinks; when it holds fast to God's power and promise, it remains above the waves.

Present troubles are bearable when we know we will find consolation in God.

We have real reasons to mourn our sin, but despair and despondency often spring from unbelief and a rebellious will. We should therefore pray and struggle against them.

Remembering God's mercies (verses 6–11)

The way to forget our misery is to remember the God who has shown us mercy.

David recognized that his suffering had been permitted by God, and this sometimes discouraged him.

Yet if troubles arrive one after another and seem to combine against us, remember that they remain subject to the Lord's appointment and government.

David regarded divine favor as the source of everything good he hoped to receive.

Let us hope and pray in the Savior's name.

One word from the Lord can calm a storm, turn midnight into midday and change bitter complaints into joyful thanksgiving.

Our confident expectation of mercy should make us more earnest in asking for it.

At last faith overcame David's fears. He determined to rely on the Lord and added the personal words, “my God.”

That thought carried him above sorrow.

Never imagine that the God who gives us life and is the Rock of our salvation has forgotten us, if we have taken refuge in his mercy, truth and power.

The psalmist struggled with discouragement until faith and hope prevailed.

Let us challenge unbelieving doubts, receive God's promises personally and then plead those promises in prayer.
classic_reading:
[Ps.42.1-Ps.42.5]
Chapter 42
The conflict in the soul of a believer.
Verses 1-5
The psalmist looked to the Lord as his chief good, and set his heart upon him accordingly; casting anchor thus at first, he rides out the storm. A gracious soul can take little satisfaction in God's courts, if it do not meet with God himself there. Living souls never can take up their rest any where short of a living God. To appear before the Lord is the desire of the upright, as it is the dread of the hypocrite. Nothing is more grievous to a gracious soul, than what is intended to shake its confidence in the Lord. It was not the remembrance of the pleasures of his court that afflicted David; but the remembrance of the free access he formerly had to God's house, and his pleasure in attending there. Those that commune much with their own hearts, will often have to chide them. See the cure of sorrow. When the soul rests on itself, it sinks; if it catches hold on the power and promise of God, the head is kept above the billows. And what is our support under present woes but this, that we shall have comfort in Him. We have great cause to mourn for sin; but being cast down springs from unbelief and a rebellious will; we should therefore strive and pray against it.
[Ps.42.6-Ps.42.11]
Verses 6-11
The way to forget our miseries, is to remember the God of our mercies. David saw troubles coming from God's wrath, and that discouraged him. But if one trouble follow hard after another, if all seem to combine for our ruin, let us remember they are all appointed and overruled by the Lord. David regards the Divine favour as the fountain of all the good he looked for. In the Saviour's name let us hope and pray. One word from him will calm every storm, and turn midnight darkness into the light of noon, the bitterest complaints into joyful praises. Our believing expectation of mercy must quicken our prayers for it. At length, is faith came off conqueror, by encouraging him to trust in the name of the Lord, and to stay himself upon his God. He adds, And my God; this thought enabled him to triumph over all his griefs and fears. Let us never think that the God of our life, and the Rock of our salvation, has forgotten us, if we have made his mercy, truth, and power, our refuge. Thus the psalmist strove against his despondency: at last his faith and hope obtained the victory. Let us learn to check all unbelieving doubts and fears. Apply the promise first to ourselves, and then plead it to God.

modern_osis:
Original heading

David endeavours to still his spirit, with hope and confidence in God.

Hope in God's light and truth

When David considered his own sin before God, he prayed that the Lord would not enter into strict judgment with him, knowing he would be condemned.

But regarding the conflict his enemies had brought upon him, he could rightly ask God to judge his cause and act on his behalf.

Even when we cannot experience spiritual joy in God, we may still rely on him.

Spiritual support remains available when spiritual delight seems absent.

God has never finally cast away anyone who trusts him, however frightened that person may be about personal spiritual condition.

We need nothing more for true happiness than the good that comes from God's favor and is included in his promises.

Those whom God leads, he directs toward his holy hill.

People who claim to follow the Spirit while turning their backs on God's appointed worship deceive themselves.

We should pray for the Spirit of light and truth, who supplies what is lacking now that Christ is no longer bodily present with his church.

He guides us along the road to heaven.

Whatever brings us joy or triumph, the Lord himself must remain the joy within it.

David returned to God as his never-failing hope.

May the Lord send out the truth of his word and the light of his Spirit to guide us in holiness, peace and salvation.

Like the suffering prophet, a Christian longs to be saved from sin as well as from sorrow.

May the heavenly wisdom shining through Jesus Christ teach us righteousness and lead us by that light and truth into the New Jerusalem.
classic_reading:
[Ps.43.1]
Chapter 43
David endeavours to still his spirit, with hope and confidence in God.
--As to the quarrel God had with David for sin, he prays, Enter not into judgment with me, if Thou doest so I shall be condemned; but as to the quarrel his enemies had with him, he prays, Lord, judge me, and in thy providence appear on my behalf. If we cannot comfort ourselves in God, we may stay ourselves upon him, and may have spiritual supports, when we want spiritual delights. He never cast off any that trusted in him, whatever fears they may have had of their own state. We need desire no more to make us happy, than the good that flow from God's favour, and is included in his promise. Those whom God leads, he leads to his holy hill; those, therefore, who pretend to be led by the Spirit, and yet turn their backs upon ordinance, deceive themselves. We are still to pray for the Spirit of light and truth, who supplies the want of Christ's bodily presence, to guide us in the way to heaven. Whatever we rejoice or triumph in, the Lord must be the joy of it. David applies to God as his never-failing hope. Let us pray earnestly, that the Lord would send forth the truth of his word, and the light of his Spirit, to guide us into the way of holiness, peace, and salvation. The desire of the Christian, like that of the prophet in distress, is to be saved from sin as well as sorrow; to be taught in the way of righteousness by the light of heavenly wisdom, shining in Jesus Christ, and to be led by this light and truth to the New Jerusalem.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A petition for succour and relief.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–8Second section9–16Third section17–26
Remembering previous deliverances (verses 1–8)

Past experiences of God's power and goodness strengthen faith and provide compelling reasons for prayer during present distress.

Israel did not win its victories through human strength or merit. Success came from God's favor and free grace.

The less praise this permits us to claim, the more comfort it offers: the achievement rests on his goodness.

God fought for Israel; otherwise its people would have fought in vain.

The same applies to the establishment of the Christian church. It did not arise through human strategy or power.

Christ, through his Spirit, went out conquering and to conquer.

The One who planted the church will sustain it by the same power and love.

God's people trust and triumph in him, so let anyone who boasts boast in the Lord.

If they find comfort in his name, they should also give him all its due glory.

The church suffers and fears abandonment (verses 9–16)

Believers experience times of temptation, suffering and discouragement. The church also passes through seasons of persecution.

In such circumstances God's people may fear he has cast them off and that his truth and name are being dishonored.

But they should look beyond the human instruments of their distress and recognize that even their worst enemies can do no more than God permits.

Faithfulness under persecution (verses 17–26)

Affliction must never drive us to obtain relief through sinful compromise.

We should continue reflecting upon the truth, purity and complete knowledge of God, who searches the heart.

Hidden sin and inward motives are known to him and will be brought into account. He understands the secret thoughts beneath words and deeds.

As long as suffering does not drive us away from duty to God, we should not permit it to drive us from comfort in God either.

Be careful that prosperity and ease do not make the heart complacent and spiritually lukewarm.

The true church cannot be forced by persecution to forget God, nor will the believer's heart finally turn from him.

Henry sees the Spirit's prophecy as pointing toward people who suffered to death for their testimony to Christ.

The appeal in verses 25–26 is not based upon personal merit or righteousness but upon the plea of a needy sinner.

No one belonging to Christ will finally be rejected. Every one of them will be saved forever.

God's mercy, purchased, promised and continually supplied to believers, overcomes the doubts arising from their sins.

Let us therefore pray in faith: Redeem us for your mercy's sake.
classic_reading:
[Ps.44.1-Ps.44.8]
Chapter 44
A petition for succour and relief.
Verses 1-8
Former experiences of God's power and goodness are strong supports to faith, and powerful pleas in prayer under present calamities. The many victories Israel obtained, were not by their own strength or merit, but by God's favour and free grace. The less praise this allows us, the more comfort it affords, that we may see all as coming from the favour of God. He fought for Israel, else they had fought in vain. This is applicable to the planting of the Christian church in the world, which was not by any human policy or power. Christ, by his Spirit, went forth conquering and to conquer; and he that planted a church for himself in the world, will support it by the same power and goodness. They trusted and triumphed in and through him. Let him that glories, glory in the Lord. But if they have the comfort of his name, let them give unto him the glory due unto it.
[Ps.44.9-Ps.44.16]
Verses 9-16
The believer must have times of temptation, affliction, and discouragement; the church must have seasons of persecution. At such times the people of God will be ready to fear that he has cast them off, and that his name and truth will be dishonoured. But they should look above the instruments of their trouble, to God, well knowing that their worst enemies have no power against them, but what is permitted from above.
[Ps.44.17-Ps.44.26]
Verses 17-26
In afflictions, we must not seek relief by any sinful compliance; but should continually meditate on the truth, purity, and knowledge of our heart-searching God. Hearts sins and secret sins are known to God, and must be reckoned for. He knows the secret of the heart, therefore judges of the words and actions. While our troubles do not drive us from our duty to God, we should not suffer them to drive us from our comfort in God. Let us take care that prosperity and ease do not render us careless and lukewarm. The church of God cannot be prevailed on by persecution to forget God; the believer's heart does not turn back from God. The Spirit of prophecy had reference to those who suffered unto death, for the testimony of Christ. Observe the pleas used, ver. #(25-26). Not their own merit and righteousness, but the poor sinner's pleas. None that belong to Christ shall be cast off, but every one of them shall be saved, and that for ever. The mercy of God, purchased, promised, and constantly flowing forth, and offered to believers, does away every doubt arising from our sins; while we pray in faith, Redeem us for thy mercies' sake.

modern_osis:
Original heading

This psalm is a prophecy of Messiah the Prince, and points to him as a Bridegroom espousing the church to himself, and as a King ruling in it, and for it.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–5Second section6–9Third section10–17
The Messiah's beauty and victory (verses 1–5)

God's Spirit guided the psalmist's tongue as a skilled writer's hand guides a pen.

This psalm concerns King Jesus, his kingdom and government.

It is a shame we speak so little about him when there is more in Christ to engage our love than in any created thing.

This world's attractions continually draw our hearts away from him. We should therefore learn how far he exceeds everything else in worthiness.

Through his word, promises and gospel, God's goodwill becomes known and his gracious work begins and grows within us.

In verses 3–5, the psalmist joyfully foretells the Messiah's advancing kingdom.

The arrows of conviction trouble sinners until they are humbled and reconciled; the arrows of vengeance bring still more terrible judgment upon enemies who refuse to submit.

Those who have seen Christ's glory and tasted his grace rejoice when his word and Spirit bring former enemies and strangers under his rule.

The eternal King and his bride (verses 6–9)

The throne of this almighty King stands forever.

The Holy Spirit leads Christ's people to his cross, where they see both the evil of sin and the beauty of holiness.

None can rightly use Christ's work as encouragement to remain in sin.

The Mediator is God. Otherwise he would neither have been able to accomplish his work nor fit to wear the Mediator's crown.

The Father, as Christ's God with respect to his human nature and mediatorial office, gave him the Holy Spirit without measure.

Anointed as Prophet, Priest and King, Christ possesses the Spirit's gifts and graces in fullness and shares them with his human brothers and sisters.

The Spirit is called the oil of gladness because Christ rejoiced in accomplishing salvation.

The angels rejoice when sinners are saved; how much more does the Son himself!

As believers are conformed to Christ's holy image, they experience the Comforter's joyful influence.

The fragrance of Christ's garments pictures his excellences, the suitability of his offices and the sufficiency of his grace.

His church, composed of true believers, is compared to a queen, betrothed to Jesus by an everlasting covenant.

She is the Lamb's bride.

Her purity resembles fine linen and her costly honor resembles gold. Both her redemption and her beauty depend on the Son of God's precious blood.

The bride's holiness and the nations' hope (verses 10–17)

To share these blessings, we must listen to Christ's word and abandon sinful attachments and worldly pursuits.

He must be our Lord as well as our Savior.

Every idol must be cast away so that we can give him our whole heart.

This renunciation has a rich reward: Christ values the beauty of holiness in his church and every believer.

Grace is the Spirit's own workmanship, forming Christ's image in the soul and giving a share in divine holiness.

There is no sin in that work of grace itself; the old corrupt nature has no true glory.

The Father's gift of Christ's righteousness clothes his church.

No one comes to Christ unless brought by the Father.

The clothing and entrance of the bride picture conversion and the garments of salvation Christ gives his people.

Those who love him sincerely and remain close to him share the bride's grace, privileges and salvation.

They will all be brought to the King; not one will be forgotten.

The New Testament church, including Gentile believers, will succeed the Old Testament church in this prophetic picture.

As we look forward to eternal happiness, let us remember Christ as the only way and teach his name to generations still to come, so that his praise endures forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.45.1-Ps.45.5]
Chapter 45
This psalm is a prophecy of Messiah the Prince, and points to him as a Bridegroom espousing the church to himself, and as a King ruling in it, and for it.
Verses 1-5
The psalmist's tongue was guided by the Spirit of God, as the pen is by the hand of a ready writer. This psalm is touching the King Jesus, his kingdom and government. It is a shame that this good matter is not more the subject of our discourse. There is more in Christ to engage our love, than there is or can be in any creature. This world and its charms are ready to draw away our hearts from Christ; therefore we are concerned to understand how much more worthy he is of our love. By his word, his promise, his gospel, the good will of God is made known to us, and the good work of God is begun and carried on in us. The psalmist, ver. #(3-5), joyfully foretells the progress and success of the Messiah. The arrows of conviction are very terrible in the hearts of sinners, till they are humbled and reconciled; but the arrows of vengeance will be more so to his enemies who refuse to submit. All who have seen his glory and tasted his grace, rejoice to see him, by his word and Spirit, bring enemies and strangers under his dominion.
[Ps.45.6-Ps.45.9]
Verses 6-9
The throne of this almighty King is established for ever. While the Holy Spirit leads Christ's people to look to his cross, he teaches them to see the evil of sin and the beauty of holiness; so that none of them can feel encouragement to continue in sin. The Mediator is God, else he had been neither able to do the Mediator's work, nor fit to wear the Mediator's crown. God the Father, as his God in respect to his human nature and mediatorial offices, has given to him the Holy Spirit without measure. Thus anointed to be a Prophet, Priest, and King, Christ has pre-eminence in the gladdening gifts and graces of the spirit, and from his fulness communicates them to his brethren in human nature. The Spirit is called the oil of gladness, because of the delight wherewith Christ was filled, in carrying on his undertakings. The salvation of sinners is the joy of angels, much more of the Son. And in proportion as we are conformed to his holy image, we may expect the gladdening gifts influences of the Comforter. The excellences of the Messiah, the suitableness of his offices, and the sufficiency of his grace, seem to be intended by the fragrance of his garments. The church formed of true believers, is here compared to the queen, whom, by an everlasting covenant, the Lord Jesus has betrothed to himself. This is the bride, the Lamb's wife, whose graces are compared to fine linen, for their purity; to gold, for their costliness: for as we owe our redemption, so we owe our adorning, to the precious blood of the Son of God.
[Ps.45.10-Ps.45.17]
Verses 10-17
If we desire to share these blessings, we must hearken to Christ's word. We must forget our carnal and sinful attachments and pursuits. He must be our Lord as well as our Saviour; all idols must be thrown away, that we may give him our whole heart. And here is good encouragement, thus to break off from former alliances. The beauty of holiness, both on the church and on particular believers, is, in the sight of Christ, of great price, and very amiable. The work of grace is the workmanship of the Spirit, it is the image of Christ upon the soul, a partaking of the Divine nature. It is clear of all sin, there is none in it, nor any comes from it. There is nothing glorious in the old man or corrupt nature; but in the new man, or work of grace upon the soul, every thing is glorious. The robe of Christ's righteousness, which he has wrought out for his church, the Father imputes unto her, and bestows upon her. None are brought to Christ, but those whom the Father brings. This notes the conversion of souls to him. The robe of righteousness, and garments of salvation, the change of raiment Christ has put upon her. Such as strictly cleave to Christ, loving him in singleness of heart, are companions of the bride, who partake of the very same grace, enjoy the same privileges, and share in one common salvation. These, every one, shall be brought to the King; not one lost or left behind. Instead of the Old Testament church, there shall be a New Testament church, a Gentile church. In the believing hope of our everlasting happiness in the other world, let us always keep up the remembrance of Christ, as our only way thither; and transmit the remembrance of him to succeeding generations, that his name may endure for ever.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesConfidence in God.1–5An exhortation to behold it.6–11
Confidence in God's presence (verses 1–5)

This psalm encourages hope and trust in God's power, Providence and gracious presence with his church, even during the most difficult times.

It also speaks to our conflicts with spiritual enemies and the promise that through Christ we will overcome them.

God is a help, a present help—someone we have already experienced as our helper.

He is always near and available. We cannot desire a better refuge or find an equal among created beings.

People whose confidence rests upon unstable foundations will panic when the waters rage.

But those led to the Rock can stand securely.

The psalm gives the church joy even amid sorrow.

Its river pictures the Holy Spirit's graces and consolations, flowing throughout the church through God's appointed ordinances and bringing joy to every believer.

God promises that his church will not finally be moved.

When he dwells in our hearts and his word lives richly within us, he will establish and help us.

Let us trust him and refuse to be afraid.

Behold God's works (verses 6–11)

Look at the consequences of devastating judgments and stand in reverence before God.

At the same time, recognize the church's ultimate safety and the promise of lasting peace.

Pray that those glorious days will arrive soon.

Worship and trust our almighty Sovereign with humble submission.

Let all believers rejoice that the Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob, has been with us, is with us and will remain with us.

He is our refuge.

Take hold of this assurance and answer every fear with it:

If God is for us, who can be against us?

Let that confidence sustain us both in life and in death.
classic_reading:
[Ps.46.1-Ps.46.5]
Chapter 46
Chapter Outline
Confidence in God. | (1-5) |
An exhortation to behold it. | (6-11) |
Verses 1-5
This psalm encourages to hope and trust in God; in his power and providence, and his gracious presence with his church in the worst of times. We may apply it to spiritual enemies, and the encouragement we have that, through Christ, we shall be conquerors over them. He is a Help, a present Help, a Help found, one whom we have found to be so; a Help at hand, one that is always near; we cannot desire a better, nor shall we ever find the like in any creature. Let those be troubled at the troubling of the waters, who build their confidence on a floating foundation; but let not those be alarmed who are led to the Rock, and there find firm footing. Here is joy to the church, even in sorrowful times. The river alludes to the graces and consolations of the Holy Spirit, which flow through every part of the church, and through God's sacred ordinances, gladdening the heart of every believer. It is promised that the church shall not be moved. If God be in our hearts, by his word dwelling richly in us, we shall be established, we shall be helped; let us trust and not be afraid.
[Ps.46.6-Ps.46.11]
Verses 6-11
Come and see the effects of desolating judgments, and stand in awe of God. This shows the perfect security of the church, and is an assurance of lasting peace. Let us pray for the speedy approach of these glorious days, and in silent submission let us worship and trust in our almighty Sovereign. Let all believers triumph in this, that the Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob, has been, is, and will be with us; and will be our Refuge. Mark this, take the comfort, and say, If God be for us, who can be against us? With this, through life and in death, let us answer every fear.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The people exhorted to praise God.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–4Second section5–9
The Sovereign gathers the nations (verses 1–4)

The Lord with whom we have to do possesses awesome majesty.

The universal and absolute sovereignty of a holy God would be terrifying even to contemplate if it were not exercised through his Son from a throne of mercy.

Now it brings terror only to those who persist in wickedness.

God's people should encourage each other in joyful trust and obedience.

Sinners should submit to his authority and receive the salvation he offers.

Jesus Christ will bring Gentile nations under his rule, drawing them like sheep into the fold—not to kill them, but to preserve them.

He will transform their affections and make them willing subjects in the day of his power.

His kingdom also grants rest and security.

In its spiritual meaning the psalm teaches that the Lord himself becomes his people's inheritance.

This is the faith and submission of the saints:

“The Lord will choose my inheritance for me; he knows what is best for me better than I do.”

Praise with understanding (verses 5–9)

We should praise God frequently and generously.

Yet one rule must always govern our worship: sing praises with understanding.

Know why you are praising God, what he has done and what the service means.

Worship is not acceptable when it is mindless and unreasonable.

We should never lose sight of the purpose of Messiah's exaltation.

The prophets continually return to the conversion of the nations through the gospel of Christ.

It is empty to imagine we belong to Christ if his Spirit does not reign in our hearts by faith.

Lord, you are exalted as Prince and Savior to grant repentance and forgiveness.

Establish your kingdom in us.

Bring every thought into obedience to Christ and turn all the powers and desires of redeemed souls toward holy love, reverence and joy in you.

May praise with understanding rise from every heart both now and forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.47.1-Ps.47.4]
Chapter 47
The people exhorted to praise God.
Verses 1-4
The God with whom we have to do, is a God of awful majesty. The universal and absolute sovereignty of a holy God would be too terrible for us even to think of, were it not exercised by his Son from a mercy-seat; but now it is only terrible to the workers of iniquity. While his people express confidence and joy, and animate each other in serving him, let sinners submit to his authority, and accept his salvation. Jesus Christ shall subdue the Gentiles; he shall bring them as sheep into the fold, not for slaughter, but for preservation. He shall subdue their affections, and make them a willing people in the day of his power. Also it speaks of his giving them rest and settlement. Apply this spiritually; the Lord himself has undertaken to be the inheritance of his people. It shows the faith and submission of the saints. This is the language of every gracious soul, The Lord shall choose my inheritance for me; he knows what is good for me better than I do.
[Ps.47.5-Ps.47.9]
Verses 5-9
Praise is a duty in which we ought to be frequent and abundant. But here is a needful rule; Sing ye praises with understanding. As those that understand why and for what reasons they praise God, and what is the meaning of the service. It is not an acceptable service, if it is not a reasonable service. We are never to forget the end of Messiah's exaltation, so continually do the prophets dwell upon the conversion of the nations to the gospel of Christ. Why do we vainly fancy that we belong to him, unless the Spirit reign in our hearts by faith? Lord, is it not thy glory and delight to give repentance to Israel and remission of sins, now that thou art exalted as a Prince and a Saviour? Set up thy kingdom in our hearts. Bring into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ. And so sweetly constrain all the powers and faculties of the souls of thy redeemed, into holy love, fear, and delight in thee, that praise with the understanding may rise from every heart, both here and for ever, to Thee, our God.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The glories of the church of Christ.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–7Second section8–14
The beauty of God's city (verses 1–7)

Jerusalem is the city of God.

Henry teaches that those belonging to the spiritual Jerusalem are the ones who truly honor him on earth.

Happy is any kingdom, city, family or individual heart where God is great and God is everything.

There he is known.

The more clearly we understand his greatness, the more praise should arise from us.

Sin has disfigured the earth.

Therefore the place adorned with divine holiness could rightly be called the joy of the whole earth—a reason for all nations to rejoice that God truly dwells with humanity.

The earthly kings feared it.

The destruction of an entire fleet in a storm provides a fitting picture of paganism being overcome by the Spirit of the gospel.

Both require the Lord's mighty power.

The security and everlasting guide of the church (verses 8–14)

God's people should learn from every glorious act of his favor.

Let such deliverances strengthen faith in his word, encourage hope in the church's stability and fill our minds with worthy thoughts of him.

Every stream of mercy flowing toward us must be traced back to the fountain of his loving-kindness.

Give God the glory for everything great he has done.

Every member of the church should take comfort from what the Lord does for his people.

Consider the church's beauty, strength and safety.

It is founded upon Christ the Rock, fortified by divine power and guarded by the One who never slumbers or sleeps.

His appointed ordinances are like palaces, and his promises are like defensive walls.

Recognize these blessings, be encouraged to belong to his church and tell others about them.

The God who has done great things for us does not change in his love or care.

If he is our God, he will guide and preserve us to the end.

He will take us beyond death's reach, so that death cannot finally harm us, and bring us into a life where death no longer exists.

Chapter 48
The glories of the church of Christ.
Verses 1-7
Jerusalem is the city of our God: none on earth render him due honour except the citizens of the spiritual Jerusalem. Happy the kingdom, the city, the family, the heart, in which God is great, in which he is all. There God is known. The clearer discoveries are made to us of the Lord and his greatness, the more it is expected that we should abound in his praises. The earth is, by sin, covered with deformity, therefore justly might that spot of ground, which was beautified with holiness, be called the joy of the whole earth; that which the whole earth has reason to rejoice in, that God would thus in very deed dwell with man upon the earth. The kings of the earth were afraid of it. Nothing in nature can more fitly represent the overthrow of heathenism by the Spirit of the gospel, than the wreck of a fleet in a storm. Both are by the mighty power of the Lord.
[Ps.48.8-Ps.48.14]
Verses 8-14
We have here the improvement which the people of God are to make of his glorious and gracious appearances for them. Let our faith in the word of God be hereby confirmed. Let our hope of the stability of the church be encouraged. Let our minds be filled with good thoughts of God. All the streams of mercy that flow down to us, must be traced to the fountain of His loving-kindness. Let us give to God the glory of the great things he has done for us. Let all the members of the church take comfort from what the Lord does for his church. Let us observe the beauty, strength, and safety of the church. Consider its strength; see it founded on Christ the Rock, fortified by the Divine power, guarded by Him who neither slumbers nor sleeps. See what precious ordinances are its palaces, what precious promises are its bulwarks, that you may be encouraged to join yourselves to it: and tell this to others. This God, who has now done such great things for us, is unchangeable in his love to us, and his care for us. If he is our God, he will lead and keep us even to the last. He will so guide us, as to set us above the reach of death, so that it shall not do us any real hurt. He will lead us to a life in which there shall be no more death.

A warning for everyone (verses 1–5)

Few psalms begin more solemnly, because few truths are more important.

Everyone should listen and apply this teaching personally.

Poor people may be harmed by excessive longing for wealth, just as wealthy people may be harmed by excessive enjoyment of it.

The psalmist first applied the warning to himself, which is the right way to approach divine truth.

Before he described the foolishness of worldly self-confidence, he explained the security that comes through trusting God instead of possessions.

At judgment, the sins of our past lives will confront us.

Worldly sinners will rightly fear.

But why should someone fear death if God is with that person?

The folly of trusting wealth (verses 6–14)

A person may possess riches and still have a heart enlarged by love, gratitude and obedience, using wealth for good.

It is not merely having possessions that makes someone worldly, but treating them as the highest good.

Worldly people may think occasionally about God, yet their deepest, most lasting thoughts center on earthly things.

Even the richest person cannot buy back the life of a beloved friend.

The psalm points beyond that limit toward the eternal redemption accomplished by the Messiah.

Redeeming a soul costs more than any earthly fortune.

But once Christ has accomplished that redemption, it never needs to be repeated.

The Redeemer rose before seeing corruption and lives forever (Revelation 1:18).

How foolish to sell one's soul for possessions that can never purchase its salvation!

No wealth can protect its owner from death.

Yet one generation after another praises the wisdom of making money the goal of life.

Even professing Christians imitate the rich fool in Luke 12:16–21.

Death will confront the proud sinner with the question: Where are all your possessions and splendor now?

At resurrection, the upright will be raised to honor while unrepentant sinners face everlasting shame (Daniel 12:2).

We should assess riches and holiness now as they will appear then.

The beauty of holiness alone cannot be damaged by the grave.

Hope beyond death (verses 15–20)

Believers need not fear death.

The enormous inequalities of wealth and rank we see during life disappear at the grave.

But differences in people's spiritual condition become enormously significant at and after death.

God, who created human life, is also able to redeem it from eternal ruin.

Believers are tempted to envy worldly prosperity.

Other people praise someone who has built a large fortune and secured an influential family.

Yet what does human approval matter if God condemns us?

People rich in the Spirit's grace and comfort possess something death cannot take away. Indeed, death will bring them into a fuller enjoyment of it.

By contrast, worldly possessions must all be left behind.

We brought nothing into the world and can take nothing away.

Gaining the whole world is worthless if it means losing one's soul.

Without true heavenly wisdom, a person fails to live and die as a being made in God's image.

Yet some people still prefer the lot of the wealthy sinner to that of poor Lazarus, even when they consider the life to come.

How deeply we need the teaching of the Holy Spirit, since our supposed wisdom can still make us foolish about what matters most!

Chapter 49
Chapter Outline
A call for attention. | (1-5) |
Folly of worldlings. | (6-14) |
Against fear of death. | (15-20) |
Verses 1-5
We seldom meet with a more solemn introduction: there is no truth of greater importance. Let all hear this with application to ourselves. The poor are in danger from undue desire toward the wealth of the world, as rich people from undue delight in it. The psalmist begins with applying it to himself, and that is the right method in which to treat of Divine things. Before he sets down the folly of carnal security, he lays down, from his own experience, the benefit and comfort of a holy, gracious security, which they enjoy who trust in God, and not in their worldly wealth. In the day of judgment, the iniquity of our heels, or of our steps, our past sins, will compass us. In those days, worldly, wicked people will be afraid; but wherefore should a man fear death who has God with him?
[Ps.49.6-Ps.49.14]
Verses 6-14
Here is a description of the spirit and way of worldly people. A man may have wealth, and may have his heart enlarged in love, thankfulness, and obedience, and may do good with it. Therefore it is not men's having riches that proves them to be worldly, but their setting their hearts upon them as the best things. Worldly men have only some floating thoughts of the things of God, while their fixed thoughts, their inward thoughts, are about the world; that lies nearest the heart. But with all their wealth they cannot save the life of the dearest friend they have. This looks further, to the eternal redemption to be wrought out by the Messiah. The redemption of the soul shall cost very dear; but, being once wrought, it shall never need to be repeated. And he, the Redeemer, shall rise again before he sees corruption, and then shall live for evermore, [Rev.1.18] Re 1:18. This likewise shows the folly of worldly people, who sell their souls for that which will never buy them. With all their wealth they cannot secure themselves from the stroke of death. Yet one generation after another applaud their maxims; and the character of a fool, as drawn by heavenly Wisdom itself, [Luke.12.16-Luke.12.21] Lu 12:16-21, continues to be followed even among professed Christians. Death will ask the proud sinner, Where is thy wealth, thy pomp? And in the morning of the resurrection, when all that sleep in the dust shall awake, the upright shall be advanced to the highest honour, when the wicked shall be filled with everlasting shame and contempt, [Dan.12.2] Da 12:2. Let us now judge of things as they will appear in that day. The beauty of holiness is that alone which the grave cannot touch, or damage.
[Ps.49.15-Ps.49.20]
Verses 15-20
Believers should not fear death. The distinction of men's outward conditions, how great soever in life, makes none at death; but the difference of men's spiritual states, though in this life it may seem of small account, yet at and after death is very great. The soul is often put for the life. The God of life, who was its Creator at first, can and will be its Redeemer at last. It includes the salvation of the soul from eternal ruin. Believers will be under strong temptation to envy the prosperity of sinners. Men will praise thee, and cry thee up, as having done well for thyself in raising an estate and family. But what will it avail to be approved of men, if God condemn us? Those that are rich in the graces and comforts of the Spirit, have something of which death cannot strip them, nay, which death will improve; but as for worldly possessions, as we brought nothing into the world, so it is certain that we shall carry nothing out; we must leave all to others. The sum of the whole matter is, that it can profit a man nothing to gain the whole world, to become possessed of all its wealth and all its power, if he lose his own soul, and is cast away for want of that holy and heavenly wisdom which distinguishes man from the brutes, in his life and at his death. And are there men who can prefer the lot of the rich sinner to that of poor Lazarus, in life and death, and to eternity? Assuredly there are. What need then we have of the teaching of the Holy Ghost; when, with all our boasted powers, we are prone to such folly in the most important of all concerns!

God's glory and judgment (verses 1–6)

This psalm instructs us about Christ's coming and the final judgment, when God will call humanity to account.

The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of judgment.

Everyone needs to know how to worship the Lord in spirit and truth.

On the great day, those who refused to hear God's law will be made to hear his judgment.

Happy are people who enter the covenant of grace through faith in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice and show genuine love through righteous conduct.

God rejects people who rest upon outward religious performances.

He graciously receives those who seek him sincerely.

Only through Christ, the great Sacrifice, can anyone be accepted by God. The sacrifices of the Mosaic law had value only through their relation to him.

God's judgments are righteous and true.

Even sinners' consciences will finally acknowledge his justice.

Prayer and thanksgiving beyond empty ritual (verses 7–15)

Obedience is better than sacrifice, and loving God and neighbor is worth more than every burnt offering.

We must never rest in the performance of ceremonies—or in any external form of religion.

God demands the heart.

How could invented religious forms please him when repentance, faith and holiness are neglected?

In distress, we should call upon the Lord through earnest prayer.

Even when suffering comes under his providential correction, it should drive us toward him, not away from him.

We should acknowledge him in all our ways, depend upon his wisdom, power and goodness, and entrust ourselves wholly to him.

Thus we maintain fellowship with God, meeting difficulty with prayer and deliverance with praise.

A believing worshiper receives not only a gracious answer but also grace to thank God for that answer.

God requires sincere obedience (verses 16–23)

Hypocrisy is wickedness, and God will judge it.

People who teach God's laws to others too often live in disobedience to those same commands.

They deceive themselves by abusing God's patience and misunderstanding his character and gospel.

At final judgment, sinners' wrongdoing will be exposed completely.

God will set their sins in order—from childhood and youth through adulthood and old age—to their lasting shame and terror.

Those who have forgotten him, persisted in wickedness or neglected salvation should recognize the urgency of their condition.

The Lord's patience is extraordinary, especially considering how badly people misuse it.

If they refuse to turn, they will recognize their mistake when it is too late.

People who forget God also forget who they themselves are.

Our highest purpose is to glorify him.

Whoever offers true praise gives him glory, and such spiritual sacrifices are accepted through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Priest and the altar to whom we entrust them.

Let us praise God fervently in spirit, receive his mercy with gratitude and seek to glorify him in both words and deeds.
classic_reading:
[Ps.50.1-Ps.50.6]
Chapter 50
Chapter Outline
The glory of God. | (1-6) |
Sacrifices to be changed for prayers. | (7-15) |
Sincere obedience required. | (16-23) |
Verses 1-6
This psalm is a psalm of instruction. It tells of the coming of Christ and the day of judgment, in which God will call men to account; and the Holy Ghost is the Spirit of judgement. All the children of men are concerned to know the right way of worshipping the Lord, in spirit and in truth. In the great day, our God shall come, and make those hear his judgement who would not hearken to his law. Happy are those who come into the covenant of grace, by faith in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice, and show the sincerity of their love by fruits of righteousness. When God rejects the services of those who rest in outside performances, he will graciously accept those who seek him aright. It is only by sacrifice, by Christ, the great Sacrifice, from whom the sacrifices of the law derived what value they had, that we can be accepted of God. True and righteous are his judgments; even sinners' own consciences will be forced to acknowledge the righteousness of God.
[Ps.50.7-Ps.50.15]
Verses 7-15
To obey is better than sacrifice, and to love God and our neighbour better than all burnt-offerings. We are here warned not to rest in these performances. And let us beware of resting in any form. God demands the heart, and how can human inventions please him, when repentance, faith, and holiness are neglected? In the day of distress we must apply to the Lord by fervent prayer. Our troubles, though we see them coming from God's hand, must drive us to him, not drive us from him. We must acknowledge him in all our ways, depend upon his wisdom, power, and goodness, and refer ourselves wholly to him, and so give him glory. Thus must we keep up communion with God; meeting him with prayers under trials, and with praises in deliverances. A believing supplicant shall not only be graciously answered as to his petition, and so have cause for praising God, but shall also have grace to praise him.
[Ps.50.16-Ps.50.23]
Verses 16-23
Hypocrisy is wickedness, which God will judge. And it is too common, for those who declare the Lord's statutes to others, to live in disobedience to them themselves. This delusion arises from the abuse of God's long-suffering, and a wilful mistake of his character and the intention of his gospel. The sins of sinners will be fully proved on them in the judgment of the great day. The day is coming when God will set their sins in order, sins of childhood and youth, of riper age and old age, to their everlasting shame and terror. Let those hitherto forgetful of God, given up to wickedness, or in any way negligent of salvation, consider their urgent danger. The patience of the Lord is very great. It is the more wonderful, because sinners make such ill use of it; but if they turn not, they shall be made to see their error when it is too late. Those that forget God, forget themselves; and it will never be right with them till they consider. Man's chief end is to glorify God: whoso offers praise, glorifies him, and his spiritual sacrifices shall be accepted. We must praise God, sacrifice praise, put it into the hands of the Priest, our Lord Jesus, who is also the altar: we must be fervent in spirit, praising the Lord. Let us thankfully accept God's mercy, and endeavour to glorify him in word and deed.
